project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas Commelinaceae with canonical Tradescantia anchor set
project_scope.note: B029 closed with three canonical Central Texas Tradescantia anchors. The family lesson now teaches jointed/sheathing vegetative structure first, then the 3+3 flower plan and six-fertile-stamen Tradescantia pattern, followed by same-genus architecture/hair comparisons. Commelina remains a useful family-breadth contrast.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at a node: stems are jointed and often somewhat succulent, while alternate parallel-veined leaves form a conspicuous sheath around the stem.
family_diagnostics.flower: Flowers have 3 sepals + 3 petals. In Tradescantia the flowers are bisexual and usually radially symmetric, with 6 fertile stamens; filaments are often conspicuously bearded.
family_diagnostics.inflorescence: Tradescantia commonly bears paired, contracted cymes subtended by conspicuous leaflike or spathaceous bracts.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Start with jointed stems and parallel-veined leaf SHEATHS, then inspect flower anatomy: three sepals + three petals, 3 carpels/superior ovary and capsule. IMPORTANT: a folded SPATHE is a special Commelina flowering bract, NOT a feature of the whole family. False dayflower Tinantia has an exposed cyme above a flat bract; Tradescantia often has three similar petals with six fertile stamens.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: sheathing node → 3 sepals/3 petals → tradescantia fertile stamens vs commelina 3 fertile + 3 staminodes → true dayflower flower → true dayflower folded spathe → true dayflower leaf sheath → tinantia open bract → capsule
visual_lesson.intro: Family-first visual field guide: see JOINTED STEMS and sheathing leaves, spot THREE SEPALS and THREE PETALS, then discover how flower clusters vary: Tradescantia has typical 6 fertile stamens, Commelina has a folded SPATHE enclosing buds and 3 fertile/3 sterile stamens, and Tinantia has exposed one-sided cymes with 6 fertile stamens. Real installed Commelina examples separate spathe from leaf sheath, rather than teaching all blue flowers as the same genus.

steps.title: 1 · Start at the node
steps.look_for: An alternate parallel-veined leaf whose base wraps around a soft, jointed stem.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the strongest vegetative doorway into the family and works even when the flowers have already collapsed for the day.

steps.title: 2 · Count 3 sepals + 3 petals
steps.look_for: Three distinct sepals behind three distinct, usually showy petals.
steps.why_it_matters: This confirms the basic Commelinaceae flower plan without relying on petal color.

steps.title: 3 · Look into the spiderwort stamens
steps.look_for: Six fertile stamens; in the common local Tradescantia pattern the filaments are conspicuously hairy or bearded.
steps.why_it_matters: This separates the canonical spiderwort lesson from Commelina, where fertile stamens and staminodes are differentiated.

steps.title: 4 · Split the three canonical spiderworts
steps.look_for: Gigantea = robust with nearly glabrous lower stem; humilis = low, bushy and hairy; occidentalis = narrow-leaved with long-stalked glandular hairs.
steps.why_it_matters: This turns the family lesson into an immediately useful local species comparison instead of stopping at family ID.

steps.title: 5 · Compare the TRUE dayflower flower
steps.photo_role: two large blue petals, reduced pale third, flower family comparison
steps.image_label: Commelina erecta: three petals, two very large
steps.image_credit: Paty000 · Public domain (physically installed exact-species photo)
steps.look_for: This genuine whitemouth dayflower has TWO conspicuous BLUE petals and a much smaller third petal below. Its stamens differ from typical spiderworts: Commelina has three fertile and three sterile staminodes, not six equivalent fertile stamens. Counts need a closer, rights-cleared macro than this full flower photograph.
steps.why_it_matters: Families contain specialized flower architectures: Commelina still belongs to Commelinaceae despite unequal petal sizes and sterile staminodes.

steps.title: 5a · SPOT a real flowering SPATHE
steps.photo_role: Commelina erecta folded green spathe around buds
steps.look_for: The wide green folded bract DIRECTLY BELOW a blue flower is the SPATHE. It conceals the buds and developing seed capsule. Its long-fused margins are a C. erecta character from FNA, but a dissection is still needed to show the seam itself.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates Commelina from Tinantia: false dayflower's one-sided flower cyme sits exposed above a mostly flat bract.

steps.title: 5b · Distinguish sheath from spathe
steps.photo_role: Commelina erecta sheathing leaf base and node
steps.look_for: A leaf blade emerges from a tubular SHEATH clasping the stem; pale hairs at the sheath mouth are visible. This LEAF SHEATH is NOT the separate folded flowering SPATHE shown in the preceding lesson.
steps.why_it_matters: One of the most common confusing terms: leaf sheath = base of ordinary leaf; spathe = special bract enclosing dayflower flowers.

steps.title: 6 · Follow the flower to a capsule
steps.look_for: A superior 3-locular ovary maturing into a capsule.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit closes the family loop after the vegetative node and flower characters.

species_compare.fastest_split: Tall/robust and smooth below vs low/many-stemmed and hairy throughout the vegetative plant.
Broader robust plant with nearly glabrous lower stem vs narrower prairie plant with obvious long-stalked glandular hairs.
Low bushy hairy plant vs taller grassier plant whose internodes/peduncles are especially glandular.

comparisons.title: Commelinaceae vs Poaceae
comparisons.rule: Both may have parallel-veined sheathing leaves, but Commelinaceae has showy 3-sepal/3-petal flowers and a superior capsule; Poaceae centers on ligules and spikelets with glumes, lemma and palea.

comparisons.title: Commelinaceae vs Iridaceae
comparisons.rule: Iridaceae commonly presents 6 similar tepals and an inferior ovary; Commelinaceae separates the perianth into 3 sepals + 3 petals and has a superior ovary.

comparisons.title: Tradescantia vs Commelina
comparisons.rule: Tradescantia has 6 fertile stamens in the FNA genus treatment; Commelina commonly has 3 fertile stamens with 3 staminodes and a strongly bilateral flower.

comparisons.title: Commelina erecta vs Tinantia anomala — real flowering bract comparison
comparisons.rule: Commelina erecta flowers come from a folded green SPATHE with long-joined margins; Tinantia anomala flowers occupy a largely exposed ONE-SIDED CYME subtended by a mostly FLAT/open leaflike bract. Both can have two large blue petals; verify their stamens: Commelina 3 fertile + 3 staminodes, Tinantia 6 fertile with most filaments bearded.

comparisons.title: Spathe vs sheath — these are not the same plant part
comparisons.rule: SHEATH = the basal portion of an ordinary leaf wrapping a stem/node. SPATHE = a modified bract surrounding an inflorescence (like the folded green enclosure around Commelina flowers). Do not label every green folded node cover a spathe.

visual_lesson.caveat: The flowers are short-lived, flower color overlaps among Tradescantia species, and regional hybridization can blur one-character IDs. Use multiple characters—especially architecture, leaf width, hair type, bracts and sepals. Three new/relinked Commelina images are physically installed and openly licensed. The existing Calvin field view is private-user photo; Nathan Taylor's close-up and Joey's Tinantia macro are CC BY-NC and not silently added to unrestricted family cards. The spathe seam, filament hair anatomy and mature capsule still need calibrated, individually verified macro/arrow photography.

curation_status.commelina_family_upgrade: 2026-10-14: Public-domain flower + two CC BY 4.0 physically installed exact Commelina erecta photos selected to explain unequal petals, fused spathe versus leaf sheath, and comparison to Tinantia; no new family-wide false generalizations, no range edits.

species.look_for: Usually one-stemmed at the base, robust and tall; lower stem essentially glabrous, upper internodes finely hairy; relatively broad strap-shaped foliage.
Low and many-stemmed at ground level; vegetative shoots and blades conspicuously hairy, becoming strongly glandular toward the inflorescence.
Taller prairie form with narrow grassier leaves and conspicuous long-stalked glandular hairs on internodes, peduncles and sepals.

canonical_anchor_set.comparison_warning: Flower color overlaps heavily across spiderworts. Start with architecture, leaf width and hair type, then use inflorescence bracts and sepals to confirm.
